newsitem.title: USA: Korea peace talks delayed in New York.
newsitem.headline: Korea peace talks delayed in New York.

text.p: The resumption of crucial talks between the United States and the two Koreas was delayed for several hours on Friday and North Korean officials said they had to consult with their government in Pyongyang.

The meeting, to secure North Korea's agreement to join in four-party peace negotiations that would also include China, had been scheduled to resume at 10 a.m. (1400 GMT). But U.S. officials said the North Koreans delayed the start until 4 p.m. (2000 GMT).
The three delegations held an inconclusive meeting on Wednesday in New York but all sides reported progress and said they hoped to settle the issue when they resumed on Friday.

A spokesman for North Korea's mission to the United Nations, who declined to be identified, told Reuters after his country's team failed to arrive on Friday morning: "We need to contact with capitals." Asked if there was a problem, he said: "I cannot say anything in connection with that."
U.S. spokesman Ken Bailies said only that the Americans had been informed the North Koreans would be late. "They told us they are arriving. They are arriving late," he said.
Bailies declined to say if the U.S. side thought there was a serious problem. "Our intention is to meet today," he said.

The meeting was called to hear Pyongyang's formal response to a year-old U.S.-South Korean proposal for peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing the fraying armistice with a peace treaty.

North Korea began Wednesday's meeting by essentially accepting the peace talks proposal but then tied that acceptance to a new demand for international assistance to meet severe food shortages, U.S. officials told Reuters.

Despite these demands, no new food aid pledges -- either from Washington or Seoul -- were expected before North Korea responds conclusively to a proposal for Korean peninsula peace talks, U.S. officials said.

U.S. officials have said Pyongyang cannot expect a massive effort to deal with its food problems until it enters peace talks and begins to defuse tensions on the volatile and heavily armed Korean peninsula.

After some scepticism in Washington and elsewhere, it has been widely accepted that impoverished Stalinist North Korea is facing serious food shortages that are likely to reach famine stage in the next two months.

North Korea and independent experts say the country needs 2.3 million tons of food this year. Pyongyang claims it can scrape together about half that amount, with the rest coming from international donors. Some U.S. analysts doubt this.
The U.N. World Food Programme recently appealed for 200,000 metric tons of food, with Washington offering one-quarter of that amount, including a $15 million contribution on Monday.
